# Column names for regression results
reg_columns <- c("Term", "Est.", "S.E.", "t stat.", "p-Value")
# Function for formatting p values
format_pvi <- function(pv) {
  return(ifelse(
    pv < 0.0001,
    "<0.0001",
    round(pv, 4) %>% format(scientific = F)
  ))
}
format_pv <- function(pvs) lapply(X = pvs, FUN = format_pvi) %>% unlist()
# Tidy regression results table
tidy_table <- function(x, terms, highlight_row = 1, highlight_color = "black", highlight_bold = T, digits = c(NA, 3, 3, 2, 5), title = NULL) {
  x %>%
    tidy() %>%
    select(1:5) %>%
    mutate(
      term = terms,
      p.value = p.value %>% format_pv()
    ) %>%
    kable(
      col.names = reg_columns,
      escape = F,
      digits = digits,
      caption = title
    ) %>%
    kable_styling(font_size = 20) %>%
    row_spec(1:nrow(tidy(x)), background = "white") %>%
    row_spec(highlight_row, bold = highlight_bold, color = highlight_color)
}

## GitHub Pages

1. Create a new repository named: `YOUR-USERNAME.github.io`
2. Add a file named `index.html` (or a `README.md`)
3. Go to **Settings → Pages**
4. Set “Deploy from a branch” and select `main` / root
5. Your site will be available at: `https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io`

I just did migrated my page to GitHub: [danielbrent.com](danielbrent.com)

## Publish Quarto to GitHub Pages

I want you to publish your page using Quarto:

1. Create a Quarto website project locally
2. Render the site (Quarto creates a `_site/` folder)
3. Configure Quarto to output to `docs/`
4. Push to GitHub and enable Pages from the `docs/` folder

This will help you get comfortable Quarto, which we'll use for problem sets.

# Econometrics

---

### What is special about econometrics relative to statistics or data science?

::: {.vcenter .bigger}

::: {.fragment}
Causality
:::

:::

## Causal research

## Motivation
> First, we believe that <span class="dblue">empirical research is most valuable when it uses data to answer specific causal questions, *as if* in a randomized clinical trial.</span> This view shapes our approach to most research questions. In the absence of a real experiment, we look for well-controlled comparisons and/or natural quasi-experiments. Of course, some quasi-experimental research designs are more convincing than others, but <span class="red">the econometric methods used in these studies are almost always fairly simple</span>.

*Mostly Harmless Econometrics*, p. xii (color added)

::: {.smaller}
[1\. This ideology inherently compares research designs to "gold-standard" of RCTs]{.dblue}

[2\. The methods are usually (relatively) straightforward (after training).]{.red}
:::

## Angrist and Pischke's FAQs<sup>[1]{.blue}</sup> 

:::{.big}
1. What is the <span class="hi">causal relationship of interest</span>?

1. How would an <span class="hi">ideal experiment</span> capture this causal effect of interest?

1. What is your <span class="hi">identification strategy</span>?

1. What is your <span class="hi">mode of inference</span>?


::: {.footnote}
[1]{.blue}</span> See *MHE*, chapter 1.
:::
:::
--- 

:::{.big}
***Note:*** Other questions also matter for developing quality research, *e.g.*,<sup>[1]{.blue}</sup>

- Why is your question <span class="hi">important/interesting</span>?
- Why is the <span class="hi">current literature</span> lacking or nonexistant?
- How do you propose to <span class="hi">advance the literature</span>?

::: {.footnote}
[1]{.blue} Credit for these questions goes to [Ed Rubin](http://edrub.in/) via [Reed Walker](https://w-reed-walker.com/).
:::
:::

---

### FAQ<sub>1</sub>: What is the causal relationship of interest? {#faq1}

- Descriptive exercises can be [very interesting and important](https://www.opportunityatlas.org/), but in modern applied econometrics, <span class="hi-red">causality is paramount</span>.

- **Why?**

::: {.fragment}

- Causal relationships directly <span class="hi-red">test theories</span> of how the world works.

- Causal relationships provide us with [**counterfactuals**]{.red}—how the world would have looked (or will look) under different sets of policies/circumstances.

- If you can't clearly and succinctly name the causal relationship of interest, then you may not actually have a research project.
:::

---

### FAQ<sub>1</sub>: What is the causal relationship of interest?

*Some classic and new examples...*

**Labor and Education**<br>How does an additional year of schooling affect wages?

**Urban**<br>How do drivers respond to increased road capacity?

**Environment**<br>How much does improved air quality increase housing values?

**Health**<br>What is the effect of exposure to lead on test scores?

## FAQ<sub>2</sub>: What is the ideal experiment for this setting? {#faq2}

:::{.big}
Describing the *ideal experiment* helps us formulate

- the <span class="dblue">exact causal relationship(s)</span>

- the dimensions we want to <span class="dblue">manipulate</span>

- the factors we need to <span class="dblue">hold constant</span>
:::

::: {.fragment}
NOTE: These *ideal experiments* are generally hypothetical and often impossible. However, if you can't describe the ideal research design, it will be hard to come up with reasonable data and research designs in real life.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Angrist and Pischke call questions without ideal experiments *fundamentally unanswerable questions* (FUQs).
:::


---

### Experimental Ideal

*Examples of potentially answerable questions...*

<!-- **Labor and Education**<br>How does an additional year of schooling affect wages? -->

<!-- **Urban**<br>How do drivers respond to increased road capacity -->

<!-- **Environment**<br>How much does improved air quality increase housing values? -->

<!-- **Health**<br>What is the effect of smoking on health outcomes -->

- **The effect of education on wages:** Randomize scholarships or incentives to remain in school.
- **Urban:** Randomly allocate road infrastructure funding.
- **Environment:** Randomly take power stations or industrial plants offline.
- **Health:** Randomly test and improve lead fixtures in homes and schools.

## FUQs

*Examples of challenging questions (potentially unanswerable?)...*<sup>[1]{.blue}</sup>

- How does gender affect eventual career paths?
- What role does race play in one's wages?

::: {.footnote}
 <sup>[1]{.blue}</sup> Courtesy of [Ed Rubin](http://edrub.in/) 
:::

---

### FUQs

- Sometimes even simple-sounding policy questions turn out to be fundamentally unanswerable.

::: {.fragment}
*Example of a fundamentally unanswerable question*:
> Do children perform better by starting school at an older age?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Proposed ideal experiment**

1. Randomize kids to start 1<sup>st</sup> grade at age 6 or 7.
2. Compare 2<sup>nd</sup> grade test scores.
:::

::: {.fragment}
<span class="hi">Problem:</span>
 Kids who start later are older in 2<sup>nd</sup> grade. Older kids do better. Do we want the effect of starting later or just being older?
:::

---

### FUQs

*Example of a fundamentally unanswerable question*:
> Do children perform better by starting school at an older age?

**Proposed ideal experiment<sub>2.0</sub>**

1. Randomize kids to start 1<sup>st</sup> grade at age 6 or 7.
2. <span class="hi-red">Control for age.</span> Compare test scores when kids are age 8.


::: {.fragment}
<span class="hi">Problem<sub>2.0</sub></span>
 The two groups will have been in school for different numbers of years (1 vs. 2). More school should mean better scores.
:::

---

### FUQ
*Example of a fundamentally unanswerable question*:

> Do children perform better by starting school at an older age?

**Central problem:** Mechanical links between ages and time in school.
<br><br>

::: {.center}
(Start Age) = (Current Age) – (Time in School)
:::

<br>

No experiment can separate these effects (for school-age children).


## FAQ<sub>3</sub>: What's your identification strategy?

:::{.vcenter .big}
This question<sup><span class="blue">1</span></sup> describes how you plan to recover/observe *as good as random* assignment of your variable of interest (approximating your ideal experiment) <span class="hi-blue">in real life</span>.
:::

::: {.footnote}
<sup><span class="blue">1</span></sup> You will hear this question asked *a lot*.
:::

---


:::{.big}
***Examples***

- Borders of implementation for daylight savings time<br>
  -[Energy consumption](https://www.mitpressjournals.org/doi/abs/10.1162/REST_a_00131)
- License plates and lucky numbers in Beijing<br>
  -[Air quality](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S004727271500016X); [Driving](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0095069619300300); [Congestion Costs](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pol.20170195) 
- Thresholds or notches in policy eligibility<br>
  -[Pensions eligibility](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.99.5.2209); [Capital subsidies](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0047272713002156); [R&D subsidies](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pol.6.4.100)
- Random judge assignments<br>
  -[Football games](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/app.20160390); [Politics](aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/pol.20170329); [Climate](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/app.20170223)
:::

---

### FAQ<sub>3</sub>: What's your identification strategy?

The term "identification strategy" goes back to Angrist and Krueger (1991).

::: {.small}
>  The variety of evidence presented in Section I establishes that compulsory schooling laws increase educational attainment for those covered by the laws. In Section II we consider whether students who attend school longer because of compulsory schooling receive higher earnings as a result of their increased schooling.  Two-stage least squares (TSLS) estimates are used in which the  source of **identification** is variation in education that results **solely from differences in season of birth-which, in turn, results from the effect of compulsory schooling laws.** The results suggest that men who are forced to attend school by compulsory schooling laws **earn higher wages as a result of their increased schooling.**

-  *Angrist and Krueger (1991)*
:::

## FAQ<sub>4</sub>: What is your mode of inference?

- Historically, inference—standard errors, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, *etc.*—has received much less attention than point estimates. It's becoming more important (more than an afterthought).

- Which **population** does your sample represent?

- How much **noise** (error) exists in your estimator (and estimates)?

- How much **variation** do you actually have in your variable of interest?

- Without careful inference, we don't know the difference between
  - 21% ± 2.3%
  - 21% ± 20.3%
